title: Chemical Reactions and Equations Workshop - Interactive study deck generated from jesc101.pdf

questions.question: Which observation from the chapter is a clear sign that a chemical reaction has taken place?
options: A change in the shape of a beaker
A substance being cut into pieces
A solid being ground into powder
questions.explanation: Page 2 lists gas evolution, colour change, state change, and temperature change as reaction indicators.

questions.question: Why is a magnesium ribbon cleaned before it is burned in air?
options: To remove the oxide layer so magnesium can react properly
To make it dissolve in water faster
To increase its mass before burning
questions.explanation: The chapter asks students to rub the ribbon with sandpaper so the surface oxide layer does not interfere.

questions.question: What is formed when magnesium burns in oxygen?
questions.explanation: The opening activity states that burning magnesium in oxygen produces magnesium oxide.

questions.question: In the zinc and dilute acid activity, the bubbles indicate the release of which gas?
questions.explanation: On pages 1-2, zinc reacting with dilute acid is used to show gas evolution; the gas formed is hydrogen.

questions.question: What visible result is observed when lead nitrate solution is mixed with potassium iodide solution?
questions.explanation: The lead nitrate and potassium iodide activity is used to show the formation of a yellow precipitate.

questions.question: Which daily-life example in the chapter is used to illustrate chemical change?
questions.explanation: Page 1 lists grape fermentation among the familiar chemical changes.

questions.question: Which statement best distinguishes a chemical change from a physical change in this chapter?
options: The identity of the original substance changes
Only the size of the substance changes
The material can always be restored by cooling
questions.explanation: The introduction emphasises that the nature and identity of the initial substance change in a chemical reaction.

questions.question: In a word equation, substances written before the arrow are called
questions.explanation: The chapter uses the word-equation format to separate reactants from products.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of converting a reaction description into a word equation first?
options: To make the reaction shorter and easier to analyse
To remove the need for formulae later
To prove that balancing is unnecessary
questions.explanation: Page 2 explains that sentence descriptions are long, and word equations provide a shorter, clearer representation.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT listed as evidence of a chemical reaction on page 2?
questions.explanation: The text explicitly lists colour, state, gas evolution, and temperature change, not shape change.

questions.question: Respiration is included in the chapter introduction because it is
options: a chemical reaction occurring inside the body
an example of only volume expansion
questions.explanation: The first page uses respiration as an everyday example of chemical change.

questions.question: Digestion is treated as a chemical process in the chapter because
options: food is transformed into different substances in the body
the body cools down during digestion
digestion is only a filtration process
questions.explanation: The introduction groups digestion with other processes where the original substance changes identity.

questions.question: When a reaction vessel becomes warmer during a reaction, the observation mainly indicates
options: a temperature change associated with reaction
that the reaction must be physical
that no new substance is formed
questions.explanation: The zinc and acid activity asks students to touch the flask and notice the temperature change.

questions.question: Which pair from the chapter is mixed to demonstrate precipitate formation?
questions.explanation: The early activities use lead nitrate solution plus potassium iodide solution to show precipitate formation.

questions.question: Which sequence best matches the textbook's learning flow?
options: Observation -> verbal description -> word equation -> symbolic equation
Redox definition -> gas test -> word equation
questions.explanation: The chapter starts from observed changes, then describes them in words, and only after that moves toward symbolic equations.

questions.question: What does the state symbol (aq) represent in a chemical equation?
options: A substance in solid crystalline form
questions.explanation: The chapter uses (aq) for aqueous solution, meaning dissolved in water.

questions.question: Which state symbol stands for a gas?
questions.explanation: Pages 3-5 list the standard state symbols used in complete chemical equations.

questions.question: What is the main difference between a skeletal equation and a balanced equation?
options: A balanced equation has equal numbers of each type of atom on both sides
A skeletal equation always includes heat terms
A balanced equation never uses formulae
A skeletal equation contains only products
questions.explanation: The chapter explains that balancing makes the atom counts equal on both sides.

questions.question: In balancing equations, what are you allowed to change?
options: Only the coefficients in front of formulae
questions.explanation: The balancing method explicitly says not to change anything inside the formula boxes.

questions.question: What is the balanced form of Fe + H2O -> Fe3O4 + H2 shown in the chapter?
questions.explanation: Pages 4-5 work this example through and end with 3Fe + 4H2O -> Fe3O4 + 4H2.

questions.question: Why must chemical equations be balanced?
options: Because atoms are conserved during a chemical reaction
Because products must always outnumber reactants
Because only balanced equations can include solids
Because balancing changes the reaction type
questions.explanation: The text ties balancing directly to the conservation of mass and unchanged atom counts.

questions.question: Which representation is the first shortened step after a sentence description of a reaction?
questions.explanation: Page 2 introduces the word equation before the symbolic equation.

questions.question: What does the symbol (s) mean in a complete chemical equation?
questions.explanation: The state-symbol table in the chapter uses (s) for solid.

questions.question: If a student changes O2 to O3 while balancing, what has gone wrong?
options: They changed the substance instead of the coefficient
They converted a product into a reactant
They only changed the physical state
questions.explanation: The chapter's box method exists to prevent altering subscripts and therefore changing the identity of the substance.

questions.question: Which part of a balanced equation shows how many units of a substance participate?
options: The coefficient written before the formula
questions.explanation: Balancing uses coefficients outside formulae to adjust atom counts.

questions.question: Which symbol shows a liquid state?
questions.explanation: The chapter lists (l) as the notation for liquid.

questions.question: What should you do immediately after writing formulae for reactants and products in an exam?
options: Balance the equation by checking atom counts
Rename all products in words again
Remove the arrow and use an equals sign
questions.explanation: The chapter's method is formulae first, then balancing by counting atoms.

questions.question: Why are state symbols especially useful in precipitation reactions?
options: They show which product is an insoluble solid
They remove the need to balance the equation
They prove a reaction is exothermic
They indicate the mass of each substance
questions.explanation: Later in the chapter, precipitation reactions are identified partly by the solid product written with (s).

questions.question: Which statement about a complete chemical equation is correct?
options: It can show reactants, products, and physical states symbolically
It only lists the names of products
questions.explanation: The chapter summary on page 14 states this directly.

questions.question: What is the balanced equation for burning magnesium in oxygen?
questions.explanation: The magnesium reaction becomes balanced by placing coefficient 2 before Mg and MgO.

questions.question: What is the defining feature of a combination reaction?
options: Two or more reactants form a single product
One compound splits into simpler substances
A metal loses shine in air
An insoluble solid dissolves in water
questions.explanation: Page 6 defines combination reactions as reactions in which a single product forms from two or more reactants.

questions.question: Which textbook reaction is used to show a combination reaction with heat release?
questions.explanation: The calcium oxide and water example on page 6 is both a combination and an exothermic reaction.

questions.question: A reaction in which heat is given out along with the products is called
questions.explanation: The chapter summary on page 14 defines exothermic reactions this way.

questions.question: Decomposition reactions are described as
questions.explanation: The chapter explicitly calls decomposition the opposite of combination.

questions.question: Which type of energy causes decomposition of silver chloride in the chapter?
questions.explanation: The silver chloride and silver bromide examples are photochemical decompositions caused by sunlight.

questions.question: What is the volume ratio of gases obtained when water is decomposed by electricity?
options: Hydrogen is collected in double the amount of oxygen
Oxygen is collected in double the amount of hydrogen
Equal amounts of nitrogen and oxygen are formed
questions.explanation: The chapter asks why one test tube collects double the gas and identifies it as hydrogen.

questions.question: Which reaction type best describes Fe + CuSO4 -> FeSO4 + Cu?
questions.explanation: Iron displaces copper from copper sulphate, so page 11 identifies it as a displacement reaction.

questions.question: Why can zinc displace copper from copper sulphate solution?
options: Zinc is more reactive than copper
Copper is more reactive than zinc
questions.explanation: The chapter states that zinc and lead are more reactive than copper and can therefore displace it.

questions.question: In a double displacement reaction, what is exchanged between the reactants?
questions.explanation: Page 12 explains that double displacement reactions involve exchange of ions between reactants.

questions.question: Why is Na2SO4 + BaCl2 -> BaSO4 + 2NaCl also called a precipitation reaction?
options: Because insoluble barium sulphate is formed
questions.explanation: The white insoluble BaSO4 formed in the reaction is a precipitate.

questions.question: Which of the following is a decomposition reaction from the chapter?
options: Mixing sodium sulphate with barium chloride
questions.explanation: Lead nitrate breaks down on heating, so it is a decomposition reaction.

questions.question: Reactions that absorb energy are known as
questions.explanation: The chapter notes that decomposition often requires energy and calls such reactions endothermic.

questions.question: Which description matches a displacement reaction pattern?
options: Element + compound -> new compound + new element
questions.explanation: This is the structural pattern of the iron-copper sulphate example.

questions.question: What is the colour of the precipitate formed in the sodium sulphate and barium chloride activity?
questions.explanation: Page 11 says the insoluble precipitate formed is white barium sulphate.

questions.question: What kind of reaction is represented by lead nitrate plus potassium iodide forming lead iodide and potassium nitrate?
questions.explanation: The chapter revisits this yellow precipitate example and points out that it also fits double displacement.

questions.question: If a substance gains oxygen during a reaction, it is said to be
questions.explanation: Page 12 defines oxidation as gain of oxygen.

questions.question: If a substance loses oxygen during a reaction, it is said to be
questions.explanation: The chapter defines reduction as loss of oxygen.

questions.question: When copper powder is heated in air, what black substance forms?
questions.explanation: The oxidation activity shows copper becoming coated with black copper oxide.

questions.question: In the reaction CuO + H2 -> Cu + H2O, which substance is reduced?
questions.explanation: Copper(II) oxide loses oxygen and is therefore reduced.

questions.question: In the reaction CuO + H2 -> Cu + H2O, hydrogen is
questions.explanation: Hydrogen gains oxygen to form water, so it is oxidised.

questions.question: Why are reactions involving both oxidation and reduction called redox reactions?
options: Because one reactant is oxidised while another is reduced
Because they always involve red-coloured products
Because they are restricted to rusting only
questions.explanation: Page 12 explicitly states that one reactant is oxidised while the other is reduced.

questions.question: Which statement about ZnO + C -> Zn + CO is correct according to the chapter?
options: Carbon is oxidised and zinc oxide is reduced
Carbon is reduced and zinc is oxidised
Both carbon and zinc oxide are oxidised
questions.explanation: Page 13 explains that in reaction (1.31), carbon is oxidised to CO and ZnO is reduced to Zn.

questions.question: Corrosion is the process in which
options: a metal is attacked by substances like moisture or acids in its surroundings
a gas forms from every reaction
questions.explanation: Page 13 defines corrosion using attack by moisture, acids, and surrounding substances.

questions.question: What is the common visible sign of rusting iron mentioned in the chapter?
questions.explanation: The text describes rusting as a reddish-brown powdery coating on iron.

questions.question: What kind of coating is mentioned for silver during corrosion?
questions.explanation: The chapter gives black coating on silver as an example of corrosion/tarnishing.

questions.question: What kind of coating is mentioned for copper during corrosion?
questions.explanation: Page 13 mentions the green coating formed on copper.

questions.question: Rancidity happens when
questions.explanation: The chapter defines rancidity as oxidation of fats and oils, changing smell and taste.

questions.question: Why do chips manufacturers flush packets with nitrogen according to the chapter?
options: To prevent oxidation of the chips
To heat the chips during packing
questions.explanation: Page 13 says nitrogen is used to reduce oxidation and prevent rancidity.

questions.question: Which storage method helps slow down rancidity?
options: Leaving food exposed to humid air
Adding more oxygen to the packet
questions.explanation: The chapter notes airtight storage as a way to slow oxidation of oils and fats.

questions.question: In the reaction 2PbO + C -> 2Pb + CO2, which statement is correct?
options: Carbon is oxidised and lead oxide is reduced
Carbon is reduced and lead is oxidised
No oxidation or reduction takes place
questions.explanation: The summary exercise on page 14 tests this exact redox interpretation.
